name: A Walk in the Woods at Nabeshima Shoto Park
tagline: Five cedar-clad huts scattered along a forest path—Kuma's village in miniature.
description:
Rather than building a single block, Kengo Kuma broke the programme into five small huts spaced along a winding path through Nabeshima Shoto Park. Each hut is clad in irregular slats of charred Japanese cedar—Kuma's signature timber language—and roofed in soft, sloping forms that echo the surrounding canopy.

The arrangement turns the act of going to the toilet into a short stroll through the woods. Sightlines stay open between huts, so the village-like layout reads as safer and more inviting than a conventional concrete block. It's a quiet rebuke to the brutalist defaults of public restroom design.

name: Eggum Rest Stop
tagline: Snøhetta's smallest building—a rest stop facing the Norwegian Sea in Lofoten.
description:
Snøhetta, the Oslo-based studio famous for the Oslo Opera House and the September 11 Memorial Pavilion in New York, designed this tiny rest stop in 2007 along Norway's Lofoten Scenic Route. It is reportedly the firm's smallest completed building. The structure terminates a simple stone-paved path that runs from a former wartime radar foundation toward the sea, framing views of the Norwegian Sea, the surrounding mountains and—in the right season—the midnight sun.

A short amphitheatre of curving stone steps doubles as a viewpoint and an informal stage. The toilet itself is plain, sturdy and weather-tight; the architecture is mostly in the staging of the view.

name: "America" – the Solid Gold Toilet
tagline: An 18-karat gold working toilet, used by 100,000 visitors at the Guggenheim.
description:
In September 2016, Italian artist Maurizio Cattelan installed America—a fully functional toilet cast in 18-karat solid gold—in a small public bathroom on the fifth floor of New York's Guggenheim Museum. Anyone with a museum ticket could line up and use it. Over the year it was open, about 100,000 people did.

Cattelan, an artist with a long history of provocations, intended the piece as a sly commentary on American excess and the populist accessibility of luxury ('one percent art for the ninety-nine percent'). In 2019, after America had moved to Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire for a special exhibition, the work was stolen in a 5am raid; it has never been recovered. The piece is now as famous for its disappearance as for its golden seat.

name: Hundertwasser Toilets, Kawakawa
tagline: A psychedelic public loo with a living roof—Hundertwasser's last completed work.
description:
In the small Northland town of Kawakawa, on the main road through town, sits a public toilet that draws 250,000 visitors a year. It was designed by the Austrian artist Friedensreich Hundertwasser, who made New Zealand his second home from 1973 until his death in 2000. Approached by Kawakawa's business association in 1997 to redesign a rundown 1960s concrete block, Hundertwasser ended up personally supervising every detail of the build—his last completed architectural project.

The result is unmistakably his: wavy roof lines, irregular ceramic tile mosaics made by local Bay of Islands College students, recycled glass bottles embedded as windows, repurposed bricks from a former Bank of New Zealand, undulating cobbled floors, and a roof planted with grasses and crowned by a living plane tree. In 2023, Heritage New Zealand designated it a Category 1 historic place—putting a public toilet, less than 25 years old, alongside Christchurch Cathedral and the Auckland War Memorial Museum.

visitorTips.title: Photo Tips

name: Toilet in Nature
tagline: A single glass cubicle in the middle of a 200m² walled meadow.
description:
Beside the tiny, unstaffed Itabu Station in rural Chiba, Sou Fujimoto designed what he calls 'the world's largest bathroom stall.' A single glass-walled toilet stands in the middle of a 200-square-metre meadow planted with grasses, clover and a cherry tree—the entire garden encircled by a two-metre-high fence of 675 vertical cedar logs.

From the bench outside, you cannot tell there's a toilet here at all. Step through the gate, walk across the wildflower field, open the door of the glass box—and the experience becomes both intensely private and dazzlingly open to the sky. Built in 2012 ahead of a local art festival, it predates the Tokyo Toilet Project by eight years and arguably inspired Shigeru Ban's transparent gambit.

name: The Great House of Easement, Hampton Court Palace
tagline: Henry VIII's communal palace toilet—seating 28 courtiers at once.
description:
When Henry VIII's court travelled to Hampton Court Palace it brought a household of around a thousand people, all of whom had to be accommodated. The solution included the Great House of Easement, a two-storey communal latrine built into the palace walls above the moat. At full capacity the structure could seat 28 courtiers simultaneously on rows of wooden boards above chutes that discharged directly into the river.

The palace also maintained a more dignified arrangement for the king himself—the Groom of the Stool, the courtier responsible for assisting Henry on a velvet-cushioned private close-stool, was among the most coveted positions at court precisely because of the intimate access it granted. The Great House of Easement survives today as part of the Historic Royal Palaces visitor route, a frank reminder of how Tudor royalty handled its plumbing.

name: Bryant Park Public Restroom
tagline: The 'Tiffany of public restrooms'—fresh flowers, classical music, rotating art.
description:
Built in 1911 by the same architects who designed the adjacent New York Public Library, the Bryant Park restroom is a Beaux-Arts granite pavilion that fell into decay by the 1960s and was closed entirely. The 1990s revival of Bryant Park—now a model of urban park renewal—brought it back. Renovations in 2006 and 2017 turned it into what The New York Times called the 'Tiffany of public restrooms.'

The interiors now feature fresh-cut flowers, classical music piped through speakers, full-service attendants, an air-conditioned interior, and a rotating selection of artworks from a 225-piece collection produced by a painters-in-residence programme. About a million people use it each year. It has been repeatedly named one of America's Best Restrooms by industry awards.

name: WHITE at Ebisu Station West Exit
tagline: A pure-white volume wrapped in aluminium louvres—the project's quietest gesture.
description:
Kashiwa Sato is one of Japan's most influential graphic designers and creative directors (he art-directed Uniqlo's global brand identity). For the Tokyo Toilet project he also designed the universal pictogram signs used across all 17 locations. His own toilet, at Ebisu Station's busy west exit, is a study in calm: a single white volume sheathed in vertical aluminium louvres that filter the surrounding noise and visual clutter.

'Clean. Reassuring. Harmonious,' Sato said of the brief. The aim was a public toilet that could be used 'as a matter of course'—blending into a frenetic urban setting rather than performing for it. In a project full of statement buildings, WHITE is a deliberate counter-melody.

name: Bukkekjerka Rest Stop
tagline: An angular mirrored toilet that disappears into a sacred Sámi rock formation.
description:
Bukkekjerka is a striking natural rock formation on the island of Andøya, used historically as a sacred site by the local Sámi people. Morfeus Arkitekter's intervention here is deliberately humble: a small toilet and shelter clad in dark, angular panels that reflect the surrounding cliffs and sky, so the building all but vanishes against the geology.

A discreet walkway leads visitors from the road to a coastal viewpoint past the toilet, ensuring the natural and cultural site remains the protagonist. It's a textbook example of the Scenic Routes program's philosophy: architecture as a hinge, not a hero.

visitorTips.description: Visit in summer for the midnight sun or autumn for the Northern Lights.

visitorTips.title: Good to Know
visitorTips.description: Respect the site's Sámi cultural significance—keep voices low and stay on paths.

name: Transparent Toilet at Yoyogi Fukamachi Mini Park
tagline: Smart glass walls turn opaque the moment you lock the door.
description:
When the Nippon Foundation launched The Tokyo Toilet project to reinvent Shibuya's public restrooms, Pritzker laureate Shigeru Ban took the most direct route to addressing the fears people have about using one: he made the walls see-through. From the outside, anyone can confirm at a glance that the stall is clean and unoccupied. Step inside, lock the door, and the smart glass instantly turns frosted, sealing the user in privacy.

At night the panels glow like coloured lanterns floating in the park, transforming a typically overlooked structure into a piece of civic theatre. Ban's design directly tackles the 'four Ks'—kusai (smelly), kurai (dark), kowai (scary), kitanai (dirty)—that long defined Japan's public toilets in the popular imagination.

visitorTips.description: Visit during daylight to see the smart-glass effect, then return after sunset for the lantern glow.

visitorTips.title: Photo Tips
visitorTips.description: Featured in Wim Wenders' film Perfect Days (2023); pair the visit with other Tokyo Toilet stops.

visitorTips.title: Accessibility
visitorTips.description: Free to use, fully wheelchair accessible, with ostomate facilities.

name: Egg Pod Toilets at Sketch
tagline: Walk-in white eggs under a rainbow ceiling, in Mayfair's most photogenic loo.
description:
Climb the curving staircase at the back of Sketch—the avant-garde restaurant set in a Georgian townhouse on Conduit Street—and you arrive at one of the world's most photographed bathrooms. A high white room is studded with milky, free-standing egg-shaped pods, each one a private unisex toilet stall. Overhead: a multicoloured rainbow LED ceiling. Around the corner: staff in Victorian housekeeper uniforms polishing fittings.

Project architect India Mahdavi designed the space when Sketch first opened in 2003 under restaurateur Mourad Mazouz. Twenty-plus years on, the pods are still the punctum of every guest's visit—an Instagram pilgrimage site by way of Stanley Kubrick.

name: Public Latrines of Ephesus
tagline: Roman-era marble benches that once seated 30 toga-clad citizens at once.
description:
Beside the Scholastica Baths in the ancient city of Ephesus—once one of the largest cities of the Roman world—runs a remarkable U-shaped marble bench with neatly cut keyhole openings. This was the public latrine, where as many as thirty Ephesians at a time would sit shoulder to shoulder in togas, conducting business and gossip while attending to nature.

Running water flowed in channels beneath the seats and at the floor for rinsing the shared cleaning sponge. Wealthier patrons paid attendants for the privilege of a warmed marble seat. The structure, dating from around the 1st–2nd century AD, has been beautifully preserved and is one of the most visited corners of the Ephesus archaeological site.

visitorTips.title: Good to Know
visitorTips.description: Wear a hat and bring water—the site is exposed and hot from May to September.

name: Utsikten Viewpoint & Rest Area
tagline: A sharp triangular concrete deck cantilevered over a Norwegian fjord valley.
description: On the Gaularfjellet Scenic Route in western Norway, the Utsikten ('the view') rest area projects a sharp triangular concrete platform out toward a panoramic fjord-and-mountain landscape. The geometry frames a single unforgettable view; a small adjoining structure houses public toilets and shelter. The combination—pure form, big nature, no fuss—has made the stop a fixture on Norwegian architecture tours.

name: Six-Star Restrooms at The Shoppes at Marina Bay Sands
tagline: Singapore's only six-star restroom—the highest rating ever issued by the RAS.
description:
Singapore takes its public toilets seriously. The Restroom Association of Singapore (RAS) rates restrooms on a three-to-six-star scale, with six stars reserved for facilities scoring above 104 out of 108 on criteria covering everything from hand-soap provision to deployment of holistic 'detect-feedback-eliminate-clean' technology. In 2018, six restrooms at The Shoppes at Marina Bay Sands became the first—and so far only—facilities in Singapore to receive the six-star rating.

The restrooms are a logical extension of Moshe Safdie's gleaming integrated resort: motion-sensor everything, gold-trimmed marble fittings, ambient music, fresh florals, and immaculate cleanliness even during peak tourist hours. The RAS Happy Toilet program is endorsed by the World Toilet Organization, headquartered in Singapore.

visitorTips.description: Take the MRT to Bayfront station (Downtown/Circle Line)—directly inside the mall.

name: Ureddplassen Memorial & Rest Area
tagline: A frosted-glass toilet that glows like an iceberg on the Arctic Ocean coast.
description:
Ureddplassen, a war memorial and rest area along Norway's Helgelandskysten Scenic Route, takes its name from a Norwegian submarine lost during World War II. Haugen/Zohar Arkitekter expanded the site with a swooping marble bench and a small public toilet whose curved, frosted-glass walls glow softly from within—an object somewhere between a fog-lit iceberg and a futuristic chapel.

The glow is intentional. Above the Arctic Circle, Ureddplassen sits in one of the best places on Earth to see the aurora borealis, and the toilet's gentle interior light is calibrated not to drown out the night sky. By day, the curved white form reads against the granite coast like an arrival from another planet.

visitorTips.title: Best Time
visitorTips.description: Best visited in summer for the midnight sun or in winter for the Northern Lights.

visitorTips.title: Getting There
visitorTips.description: Roughly a 2-hour drive south of Bodø along the Fv17.

visitorTips.title: Photo Tips

name: Sulabh International Museum of Toilets
tagline: One of the world's only museums dedicated to the history of the toilet.
description:
Sulabh International, founded in 1970 by sanitation pioneer Dr Bindeshwar Pathak, is one of India's most important grassroots organisations. Its work pulling millions out of unsafe sanitation conditions led, in 1992, to the founding of an unusual museum on its New Delhi campus: a serious, fully curated history of the toilet from 2500 BC to the present, organised across Ancient, Medieval and Modern wings.

Exhibits include replicas of Roman latrines, illustrated chamber pots from European courts, Japanese washlets, modern composting toilets, and a famous gilded model of Louis XIV's commode-throne. The museum doubles as a research centre on sanitation technology and as a platform for Pathak's advocacy work, which earned him India's Padma Bhushan and the Stockholm Water Prize before his death in 2023.

name: Selvika Rest Stop
tagline: A zig-zagging concrete path on the Arctic coast, with a toilet at the end.
description:
Along Norway's National Tourist Route Havøysund—running north of the 70th parallel, well above the Arctic Circle—Reiulf Ramstad Arkitekter designed a rest area that is mostly a journey. From the car park, a sharp zig-zag of white in-situ concrete walls descends toward the rocky shoreline, slowing visitors down and framing views of the Barents Sea. At the bottom is a small toilet block built from the same uncompromising concrete.

The project is part of Norway's celebrated Scenic Routes initiative, which commissions leading architects to design rest stops, viewpoints, and other small structures along eighteen designated roads. The Selvika rest stop has become one of the route's defining objects—architecture that turns a bathroom break into a slow, contemplative walk.

name: Amayadori at Jingu-Dori Park
tagline: A circular concrete drum wrapped in louvres—Tadao Ando's pocket-sized monument.
description:
Tadao Ando named his contribution to the Tokyo Toilet project Amayadori, which translates roughly as 'taking shelter from the rain.' The cylindrical pavilion uses a circular plan with wide overhanging eaves to create an engawa—the Japanese in-between space that mediates inside and outside—giving passers-by a place to pause as well as a place to relieve themselves.

Light filters through the vertical louvres into the central ring, where signage and sinks are arranged on a single passable loop. Ando, never one for ornament, treats this five-square-metre building with the same gravity he brings to museums and chapels: 'I sought for this small architecture to exceed the boundaries of a public toilet,' he wrote, 'to become a place in the urban landscape.'

name: Don't Miss a Sec
tagline: A working public toilet inside a one-way-mirror cube outside Tate Britain.
description:
When Italian artist Monica Bonvicini unveiled Don't Miss a Sec in December 2003, on a construction site directly opposite Tate Britain, the premise was unsettlingly simple: a fully functional public toilet enclosed in walls of one-way mirrored glass. From outside, the cube reflected the street—passers-by saw only themselves. From inside, the user looked out at every museum visitor walking past, all of them oblivious.

The title came from a hedge fund manager who said he didn't want to 'miss a sec' of trading while in the bathroom. Bonvicini was poking at the voyeurism of the art world's see-and-be-seen culture, the surveillance logic of modern life, and the question of where private ends and public begins. The piece was originally a temporary installation, but has since been re-exhibited at venues including the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art.

name: Three Mushrooms at Yoyogi-Hachiman
tagline: Three white shapes rise from the shrine forest like mushrooms after rain.
description:
Pritzker laureate Toyo Ito placed his Tokyo Toilet contribution beside the entrance to Yoyogi-Hachiman shrine, on a busy stretch of Yamate-Dori. Faced with a forested site adjacent to sacred ground, he split the building into three rounded volumes that rise from the earth like white mushrooms among the cedars.

The separation isn't only visual: each volume houses one of the three units (men's, women's, accessible), with interconnecting paths that maintain sightlines and a sense of safety. The interiors are kept deliberately bright and clean-lined, the trio reading from the street as a small grove of architectural fungi.

name: Uritrottoir Composting Street Urinals
tagline: Bright red urinals topped with flower planters—pee in, compost out.
description:
France has a centuries-old problem its citizens politely call les pipis sauvages—wild urination. In 2018, Paris ran a pilot with Nantes-based design studio Faltazi to install Uritrottoirs ('sidewalk urinals') at hotspots near Gare de Lyon, the Île Saint-Louis, and the Boulevard de Clichy. Each is a bright red waist-high box with a flower planter on top, an opening on the front, and a bed of straw or wood chips inside.

Users urinate into the straw, a sensor pings city services when the box is full, and the contents are carted off to be composted into fertiliser for municipal parks. The pilots sparked global headlines—and local protests, especially on the Île Saint-Louis—but Faltazi's circular-economy design has since spread to Nantes, Antwerp and several music festivals.

name: Transparent Toilet at Haru-no-Ogawa Community Park
tagline: The second of Ban's twin glass toilets, lit like a stained-glass box.
description:
Opened on the same day in August 2020 as its sibling at Yoyogi Fukamachi, the Haru-no-Ogawa transparent toilet uses the same trick—glass that flips from clear to opaque when the door is locked—but its three coloured cubes feel more like an installation than a single object. Ban arranges the men's, women's, and accessible units as a small constellation in the park, each lit at night in a different hue.

The pair were the first toilets unveiled in the Tokyo Toilet Project and the ones that went viral worldwide, helping the initiative attract architects from Tadao Ando to Marc Newson over the following three years.

visitorTips.description: Best viewed at sunset when the interior LEDs come on against the fading daylight.

name: Andon at Nishihara Itchome Park
tagline: A glowing green-tinted lantern that lights its neighbourhood after dark.
description:
Architect Takenosuke Sakakura named his Tokyo Toilet contribution Andon—the traditional Japanese paper lantern—and the building lives up to the name. Three unisex cubicles are wrapped in green-tinted frosted glass, etched on the inside with a soft pattern of tree branches. By day it reads as a quiet, leaf-coloured box tucked into the park; after sunset, the structure becomes a giant lantern, the cubicles glowing from within and illuminating the surrounding paths.

The colour is no accident. Greenery is famously rare in central Tokyo's smaller pocket parks, and Sakakura's lantern conjures it through light alone.

name: Tofuku-ji Tōsu
tagline: Japan's oldest surviving toilet—a 600-year-old Zen monks' communal latrine.
description:
Tucked among the sub-temples of Tofuku-ji, one of Kyoto's Five Great Zen temples, the Tōsu is an unassuming wooden hall that holds an extraordinary distinction: it is Japan's oldest surviving toilet. Built during the Muromachi period (early 15th century) for the monastery's resident monks, it is a Designated Important Cultural Property of Japan.

Inside, a long row of recessed square pits in the earthen floor served the community in strict ritual silence—part of the Zen discipline of treating every bodily function as a moment of mindful practice. The building is no longer in use, but a small wooden lattice lets visitors look in from outside, peering across six centuries of monastic life.

visitorTips.description: Tofuku-ji is a 10-minute walk from JR Tofukuji Station; the Tōsu sits within the main precinct.

visitorTips.description: Free to view; the temple's main halls and gardens are paid entry.

name: Urasando Public Toilet
tagline: A mint-green hut with a copper roof, modelled on a Japanese tea house.
description:
Industrial designer Marc Newson—better known for chairs, aircraft interiors and Apple Watches—made his architectural debut with this tea-house-inspired toilet on a quiet side street near Meiji Jingumae. The minimalist hut with its sweeping copper roof references the simple geometries of traditional Japanese teahouses and shrine outbuildings, treated with a contemporary minty palette.

The copper, untreated, will weather over decades into a soft green patina, weaving the building gradually into Tokyo's urban fabric. Inside, the fittings are characteristically Newson—rounded edges, precise details, soft lighting—turning a utilitarian box into a small object of industrial design.

name: Origata at Higashi Sanchome
tagline: A bright red origami of a building on a narrow triangular plot in Shibuya.
description:
New York–based Japanese designer Nao Tamura was given one of the trickiest sites in the Tokyo Toilet project: a tiny triangular plot wedged between a residential street and a railway line. She responded with one of the boldest objects in the series. The whole structure is painted vivid red, its thin metal eaves folded into sharp creases that recall Origata—the traditional Japanese art of decorative paper-wrapping for gifts.

Inside, the building is split into three fully independent unisex stalls so users do not have to gender themselves at a door before entering. Tamura, drawing on her years living in New York's LGBTQ+ community, designed the toilet explicitly as a safer space for people across the gender spectrum. The thin red eaves required new construction techniques—structural steel sheets rolled to a 20mm thickness—to keep the origami crispness Tamura wanted.

visitorTips.description: Three-minute walk from Higashi Station (Tokyo Metro Fukutoshin line) or 8 minutes from Ebisu.

visitorTips.title: Best Time
visitorTips.description: Catch it at sunset—the red glows against the surrounding grey buildings.

visitorTips.title: Accessibility
visitorTips.description: All three stalls are unisex; each is fully accessible and equipped for stoma users.

visitorTips.title: Getting There
visitorTips.description: Combine with the nearby Ebisu Park (Katayama) and Ebisu Station West (Sato) toilets.
